increasingly vulnerable to various forms of denial-of-service attacks. Attackers can achieve this by overwhelming CPS components with excessive traffic, thereby preventing normal operations. This study introduces a novel flooding attack called Random Flooding (RF), which leverages the flooding mechanism inherent in the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) within CPS. Unlike the well-known TCP SYN flood attack, RF exploits a different vulnerability. The attack proceeds in two phases: first, it deactivates the CPS's firewall; second, it generates flood traffic by abusing TCP options features, specifically `TCP_MAXSEG` and `TCP_WINDOW_SCALE`, which can generate multiple packets from a single data segment. We implemented and assessed this attack on a typical TCP/IP-based CPS environment using OPNET, simulating an Industrial Control System (ICS) with a SCADA protocol. Our approach successfully flooded the CPS using merely 100 packets, accounting for all incoming traffic. This RF attack imposes significant burdens on the CPS, drastically increasing queuing delays for legitimate packets and rendering the system unresponsive. As a result, the CPS experienced a 100% denial-of-service. In contrast, our experiments demonstrate that a proposed Defense Against Random Flooding (DARF) mechanism effectively mitigates this attack by blocking only the firewall's processing time. Furthermore, the DARF does not impede the functionality of CPS packets. These findings confirm that RF creates a severe denial-of-service while DARF successfully defends against it without affecting CPS performance. Finally, we propose an open-source framework for CPS security evaluation that utilizes a real-world ICS simulation platform. This framework enables the implementation and testing of DARF alongside other attacks and defenses, facilitating the validation of CPS security measures. Our research also reveals that DARF can be adapted to counter other flooding attacks. The source code is available at https://github.com/ahmedgaber2/DARF. We anticipate that this work will serve as a foundation for future DARPF CPS security evaluations. Additionally, this study is the first to evaluate an open-source DARPF CPS security framework. The source code is also accessible via https://github.com/ahmedgaber2/DARF. Our findings indicate that RF causes catastrophic denial-of-service, whereas DARPF CPS security frameworks successfully defend against it. This research paves the way for future DARPF CPS security evaluations using the DARPF CPS security framework. It is also the first to introduce a DARPF CPS security framework through this study. We demonstrate that the average dynamic landscape in the large system limit corresponds to a specific slice of a manifold defined by a family of hyperbolic Riemann surfaces. This finding generalizes our earlier result regarding real landscapes. Furthermore, we show that key statistical properties of the landscape in both real and complex cases emerge from the theory of automorphic forms. The linear color dielectric Hamiltonian incorporates confinement potential and a novel color-electric field, with the latter governed by a novel covariant color-electric displacement vector, $B_a^\mu$, which varies locally in both color and spatial domains. The equation of motion for $B_a^\mu$ establishes a direct link between confinement and the emergent color-electric field. Furthermore, the model demonstrates an energy-dependent hadronization mechanism. The specific parameters of the color-electric field and associated Hamiltonian are determined through experimental data regarding the transverse momentum distributions of charged pions and protons. The analysis reveals a reduced hadronization temperature of approximately 170 MeV for the lightest hadrons, alongside an energy-dependent enhancement in the production of charged pions and protons. These findings indicate an increase in the multiplicity of both pion and proton yields by factors of 2 and 3, respectively, when comparing the highest to the lowest energy collisions. These findings offer a qualitative explanation for the rising jet suppression ratio, $R_{AA}$, observed in Pb-Pb collisions across the RHIC and LHC energy ranges. Additionally, an inverse relationship is established between jet suppression and charged pion/proton yields in both central and peripheral collisions within the energy scan. Finally, these results align with the thermal interpretation of the medium, supporting a scenario characterized by color screening and the formation of a colored plasma. This enhanced multiplicity of jets and charged hadrons offers a promising pathway to unravel the intricate dynamics of high-energy heavy-ion collisions. The model's applicability extends to high-energy hadronization phenomena in high-energy hadron–nucleus and nucleus-nucleus collisions. In these extensions, the model parameters are fixed by a combined fit to multiplicity and transverse momentum spectra of charged hadrons. Quantitatively, the model achieves a good fit for both multiplicity and transverse momentum distributions of charged hadrons produced in Pb-Pb collisions at various energies across RHIC and LHC, as well as in Au-Au collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider. These findings offer a fresh perspective on analyzing high-energy hadronization and jet suppression. Through this approach, a reduced effective hadronization temperature is derived for both light hadrons (pions and protons) and jet suppression, relative to their respective collision energies. This methodology provides a fresh avenue for investigating high-energy hadronization and associated physical phenomena

the travel-time method utilizes observed acoustic wave propagation speeds to detect lateral variations in convective velocities, offering a means to constrain the characteristics of the near-surface turbulence layer. This approach relies on linear tomography, which inverts travel-time measurements to determine velocity fields. **Aims.** This study introduces an inversion algorithm based on ridge regression, a regularization technique that mitigates the tomographic ill-posedness by minimizing the $\ell_2$ norm of the solution. **Methods.** We apply this method to synthetic data generated by three linear involutionary processes varying in noise levels and source characteristics. The inverted velocity fields are compared against the true input fields. The optimized ridge regression results are validated against both unoptimized versions and linear tomography outcomes. **Results.** The results demonstrate that the optimized convectively turbulent velocity field can be reliably reconstructed from observed travel times. The optimized inversion yields a velocity field that closely matches the true field, exhibiting a correlation coefficient exceeding 0.95. This field remains robust across diverse sources and noise realizations. Compared to linear tomography, the optimized inversion significantly reduces the $\ell_2$ residual of the tomographic system and consistently produces smoother solutions. **Conclusions.** The study confirms that an accurate reconstruction of the near-surface velocity field is achievable when a reasonable model of the travel-time system's covariance is available. This field is highly correlated with the input field, yielding a tomographic residual approximately ten times smaller than that of linear inversion. The optimized inversion's performance is validated by successfully recovering both a realistic realistic convectively turbulent velocity field and a highly structured field. Finally, the method's application to synthetic solar data is presented. **Conclusions.** The research confirms that a reliable reconstruction of the near-surface velocity field is possible if a reasonable covariance model of the travel-time system is available. The field is highly correlated with the true convectively turbulent velocity field, resulting in a tomographic residual roughly ten times lower than that of linear inversion. The optimization's effectiveness is validated by successfully recovering both a realistic realistic convectively turbulent velocity field and a highly structured field. , and International Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) Collaborations have jointly published results from a four-year NANOGrav observation period, addressing continuous gravitational waves (CGWs) directed at the Hubble Tauri (HT) binary system. This study evaluates the temporal stability of HT's orbital period, denoted as $P_b$, by analyzing the amplitude and phase time series of the gravitational wave (GW) signal within the data. To quantify CGW-induced variations in $P_b$, we model the orbital period evolution as a quadratic function of time, $P_b(t) = P_b(0) + \dot{P}_b(0)t + \ddot{P}_b(0)t^2$, where $P_b(0)$ represents the initial orbital period, $\dddot{P}_b(0)$ denotes the period decay rate, and $\dddot{P}_b(0)$ signifies the second time derivative of the period. We establish the relationship between the CGW strain amplitude and the CGW energy density relative to the background, given by $f_G = \ddot{P}_b(0)/2$, as well as the CGW induced orbital period decay rate, represented by $\dot{P}_{GW}(0) = P_b(0) - \dddot{P}_b(0)/3$. To detect CGW signals in CGW-induced changes of $P_b(t)$, we apply the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) method to four-year data spanning 2016 to 2020. Our findings reveal no evidence of CGW presence in CGW-induced variations of $P_b(t)$ across the entire search frequency band, from 0.0001 to 0.004 Hz. We have constrained the limits on the CGW energy density and the amplitude of CGW-induced variations in $P_b(t)$ throughout the observation period. This work represents the first attempt to detect CGWs using PTA data by fitting CGW-induced orbital period variations and demonstrates the feasibility of such searches. Our results provide upper limits on the CGW energy density and CGW-induced orbital period variations for the HT binary system, contributing to the broader effort to detect CGWs via PTA observations of HT binarity. These findings also contribute to the investigation of the CGW background. Furthermore, we have developed a Python code, ptsearch, to identify CGWs in PTA data. We present a detailed description of the code's methodology

Although non-interactive solutions offer superior scalability for large model sizes, they are restricted to specific tasks such as linear regression, optimization, and training deep neural networks (DNNs). This paper introduces a novel, task-agnostic, and parameter-efficient approach utilizing an intermediate latent representation. This study investigates the automatic classification of names from the current Ethiopian Civil Registration System (CRS) census using a pronoun-guided, unsupervised cluster analysis method. We test the validity of this approach by comparing our proposed semi-classical technique against direct classical simulations that account for gravity and quantum pressure. Leveraging recent advances in classical algorithms capable of generating long-lived DM condensate configurations, we demonstrate that these methods produce time-averaged density profiles consistent with previous studies in the same ultra-light DM regime. Additionally, we examine the connection between our semi-classical model and the quantum field-theoretic approach to DM, investigating how the former approximates the latter within the context of DM condensates. Acknowledging the current limitation of semi-classical methods in accurately representing quantum evolution during non-adiabatic transitions, we recommend that ultra-light DM scenarios exhibiting strong time-dependent behavior be modeled using quantum field theory. In this study, we employed the cuprate Bi$_2$Bi$_4$CuO$_6$ as a high-quality starting material to access the embedded 2D LaCuO$_2$ substructure. Using the embedded LaCuO$_2$ as a reference, we observed a one-dimensional (1D) La$_3$Cu$_2$BiO$_7$ exhibiting typical 2D cuprate-like features, specifically a flat valence band and a 2D-like CuO$_6$ octahedral framework, rather than the expected 2D LaCuO$_2$. Furthermore, La$_3$Cu$_2$BiO$_6$, a 1D LaCuO$_2$-containing derivative of BiOBr, was also examined using ARPES; it displays a 2D-like dispersed valence band and a 1D LaCuO$_2$ substructure with a distinct Fermi level position. These findings indicate that simply substituting the B site in ternary layered oxides does not invariably result in the formation of a 2D cuprate substructure. Additionally, we observed that the 1D LaCuO$_2$ in the 1D LaCuO$_2$-containing BiOBr derivative behaves as a 2D cuprate, whereas the 1D LaCuO$_2$ in the ternary oxide BiOBr behaves as a 1D cuprate. This research provides novel insights into the design and identification of materials possessing 2D cuprate quantum substructures. Furthermore, we highlight that BiOBr and BiOBr$_2$ serve as effective precursors for fabricating both 1D and 2D cuprate substructures, which may exhibit novel quantum properties. We anticipate that these findings will significantly influence the development of quantum substructures within ternary layered oxides. We also provide detailed structural and spectroscopic data in ESI-A and ESI-B to support these conclusions. This study investigates the $D^0 \to K^+ \pi^-$ and $\bar{D}^0 \to K^- \pi^+$ decays through the interference between direct decay amplitudes and those proceeding via $D^0/\bar{D}^0$ mixing and $GPPS$ terms. The analysis focuses on the invariant mass spectrum of the final state in the range of 1.1 to 2.0 GeV$^2$. Significant excesses were observed above the background near the decays of $D_2(2460)$, $D_1(2414)$, $D_{s1}(2536)$, and $\bar{D}_1(1420)$ mesons. For each peak, various $J^P GPPS$ assignments were examined to fit the line shapes, allowing for the determination of mass, width, and relative phases linked to the interference between $D$ meson and background contributions. The results indicate that the $2.412$ GeV$^2$ peak is best described as a pure state with $J^P=1^-$, whereas the 2.460 GeV$^2$ peak favors interpretations involving two distinct resonances. Additionally, the $D_{s1}(2536)$ meson was confirmed to possess spin $J^P=1^+$. This study provides novel findings for all identified resonances, with the $D_0^*(2400)$ mass determined with high precision. Future analysis of the full data set is expected to yield more definitive conclusions regarding the quantum numbers of the remaining new states. Cross sections were derived for the $D_0^*(2400)+$, $D_1(2414)+$, $D_2(2460)+$, $D_{s1}(2536)+$, and $D_{s2}(2317)+$ mesons. Future investigations into the properties of the newly discovered states at higher statistics will offer deeper insights into their nature. This work appears in Phys. Rev. D 84, 072003 (2011). in ideal magnetohydrodynamics (IMHD) are known to be crucial for turbulence and transport in rotating cylindrical plasmas, their specific roles and relative significance remain poorly understood. This study examines small-amplitude turbulence in cylindrical IMHD (c-IMHD) and magnetic field-free (c-MHD) systems, investigating how initial magnetic field strength, magnetic Prandtl number, and magnetic Prandtl number ratio influence the system's MHD character. Using reduced-order models for both Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids, we reveal that magnetic fields in c-IMHD fundamentally alter the MHD nature of the turbulence by generating Alfvén waves, which in turn affect energy cascade, characteristics, anomalous resistivity, and transport. Our results indicate that c-IMHD exhibits characteristics of c-MHD when these magnetic effects are suppressed, validating our hypotheses. Consequently, this demonstrates that even weak initial magnetic fields can significantly impact energy transfer and anomalous transport in rotating cylindrical plasmas. The findings from Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluid simulations align, suggesting that magnetic field effects on c-IMHD turbulence are independent of the fluid's rheological type. Given that reduced models provide accurate representations of the c-IMHD system, they serve as efficient tools for simulating its behavior. Ultimately, our findings confirm that reduced models can accurately represent the c-IMHD system by capturing the essential magnetic field effects on its turbulence. This suggests that such models are valuable for investigating magnetic field influences on IMHD systems in other plasma environments, including stellarators, toroidal devices, and astrophysical settings. Our insights also contribute to the broader understanding of how non-Newtonian fluids, characterized by shear-thinning or shear-thickening behaviors, function within the c-IMHD framework. The implications of our findings extend to various applications, including fusion energy research, astrophysics, and geophysics. This occurs because a particle moving at velocity $v$ through air experiences an upward buoyant force from displaced air, while its weight results from displaced gravitational mass; the difference between these forces is termed "dynamic buoyancy." Since this effect is accelerated by gravity, it is expected to be stronger on massive planets like Jupiter. This paper demonstrates that dynamic buoyancy is fundamentally driven by the contrast between a particle's specific mass and that of the surrounding fluid. Consequently, dynamic buoyancy reaches a maximum when the fluid's specific mass matches the particle's. As a particle's specific mass remains largely constant with altitude, the specific mass of the fluid is expected to vary with wavelength, causing differential atmospheric dispersion to peak when the fluid's specific mass aligns most closely with the particle's. For gaseous planets surrounded by neutral atmospheres, this suggests that neutral particles with dynamic specific masses near that of Jupiter's atmosphere are most susceptible to dynamic buoyancy. This insight is applied to explain observations of Jupiter's Great Red Spot's drift rate and offer recommendations for future missions. Specifically, it is shown that water particles are indeed driven by dynamic buoyancy, resulting in the most significant differential atmospheric dispersion for ice particles. Additionally, the study investigates the critical conditions under which this effect becomes more complex, such as when the fluid's specific mass varies with wavelength or altitude. Finally, the paper orients this research to further explore dynamic buoyancy and its associated differential atmospheric dispersion. Through these endeavors, it is anticipated that a deeper understanding of dynamic buoyancy will be achieved. This enhanced comprehension will facilitate the interpretation of future observations regarding neutral particles in Jupiter's atmosphere and aid in designing missions to investigate dynamic buoyancy. As a preliminary step, this article examines the specific conditions required for dynamic buoyancy to become positive. It concludes that this effect is most likely to be measurable on giant planets. Specifically, it is demonstrated that for neutral particles in Jupiter's atmosphere, dynamic buoyancy is expected to be most pronounced when the specific mass of suspended water ice is approximately 0.934 g/cm³. This finding is supported by the hypothesis that the persistence of the Great Red Spot is due to its favorable dynamic specific mass relative to that of Jupiter's upper atmosphere and the dynamic specific mass of water. This hypothesis is further validated by the observation of the Great Red Spot's persistence over time. Ultimately, this work aims to foster a deeper understanding of dynamic buoyancy and to encourage future missions to study it. Specifically,

analyze multi-level time series data, where only subset variables are observed for time series 1, while complete observations exist for remaining series under higher-level latent variables. The model includes endogenous and exogenous variables at both individual and multi-level latent dimensions. We propose a Bayesian inference algorithm utilizing the Metropolis-Hastings sampling method to estimate parameters and latent variables for time series 1, with exogenous variables at multi-level latent variables contributing to its regulation. To illustrate the model's applicability, we analyzed daily stock price data for both Apple (AAPL) Inc. and Intel (INTC) Inc. The simulation results demonstrate that our proposed model effectively captures time series 1 for both companies. Furthermore, the posterior parameter distributions for AAPL and INTC align with their respective actual price trends. Specifically, the model indicates that AAPL is positively influenced by market size and negatively by the demand index, whereas INTC is positively affected by the demand index. These findings suggest that AAPL thrives in large markets and high periods of public interest, whereas INTC performs better in small markets and low public interest periods. Additionally, the model reveals that AAPL is driven by market size and demand indices, whereas INC is primarily regulated by the exogenous variables of both Intel and Apple. Finally, the model indicates that Intel is heavily influenced by Apple's exogenous variables, implying that Intel is more susceptible to external factors and less self-driven. These insights are valuable for investors seeking to understand the external influences on these Apple Inc. products. Our results confirm that the model is effective for time series analysis when only partial time series data are available. Finally, the Bayesian sampling method employed in this work is also suitable for other time series analysis problems. However, it is important to note that the Metropolis-Hastings sampling algorithm is computationally intensive and may be unsuitable for large-scale problems. Our future research will focus on developing more efficient sampling algorithms to address this limitation. Specifically, for an abelian topological group $A$ and a family $\mathcal F$ comprising its continuous homomorphisms into the circle group $\mathbb T$, we treat $(A,+)$ equipped with $\mathcal F$ as a continuous logic structure $M$. We demonstrate that the Löwenheim-Skolem-Tarski theorem allows us to construct the dual group of $M$ inside $M$ itself. This approach offers a novel, self-contained method for establishing key properties of the Pontryagin duality theorem, particularly the part asserting that the dual of duals is isomorphic to the original group. Furthermore, this technique extends naturally to abelian groups defined on uncountable sets with the discrete topology, providing a rigorous foundation for the classical Pontryagin-duality theorem. Additionally, our framework clarifies the relationship between the topologies of dual groups and the convergence types of the relevant families $\mathcal F$. A key characteristic of this framework is the radiative breaking of both the $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry and R-parity at the TeV scale, driven by the vacuum expectation value of a $Z_2$-even right-handed neutrino. The size of this mixing angle between the dark photon and the $B-L$ mediator directly influences the magnitude of dark matter annihilation, thereby controlling its relic abundance. Similarly, kinetic mixing involving the mediator that couples to the neutrino also impacts the efficiency of neutrino flavor conversion during annihilation. We demonstrate that to achieve the correct relic density through these mediator-induced mechanisms, the $B-L$ symmetry must be spontaneously broken at a high energy scale, approximately $10^{6}\text{ GeV}$. In both scenarios, precise measurements of the relic density serve as critical inputs for detecting the dark photon. This study presents a comprehensive formula linking Hamiltonian actions on symplectic manifolds with the moment map to the conformal field theoretic data of a Toda theory—specifically, the associated Lie algebra and hyperplane arrangement. As a result, we establish a global version of Sklyanin's quantum integrable Lax matrix. This Lax matrix represents the monodromy operator acting on the equivariant cohomology of the fixed point locus within the manifold. Equivalently, it can be defined as a monodromy representation on a specific space constructed from the Lie algebra and the hyperplane arrangement, which we term Lie algebra cohomology. This cohomology space is named due to its derivation using the Chevalley-Eilenberg complex and the action of the associated Lie algebra. Finally, we demonstrate that this constructed cohomology possesses a natural Hopf algebra structure and examine its properties. These findings offer significant insights into the relationship between conformal field theory and integrable systems. Specifically, our main result yields a conformal field theoretic monodromy operator for the Toda theory and suggests the existence of an associated integrable quantum field theory. This proposed monodromy operator exhibits a monodromy representation analogous to the classical case, thereby connecting conformal field theory and integrable systems. The classical monodromy operator exhibits a factorization property inspired by the quantum monodromy operator. This property enables the natural construction of a hyperplane arrangement via conformal field theoretic data and the associated Lie algebra. This factorization property also plays a crucial role in the cohomology space. This cohomology space exhibits a remarkable property: a monodromy representation, mirroring the integrable system monodromy, which serves as a strong indicator of an associated integrable quantum field theory. Furthermore, the Lie algebra cohomology serves as a highly effective tool in conformal field theory and integrable systems, as it naturally unifies the monodromy representation with the Knizhnik-Zemitanov operator, thereby connecting conformal field theory and integrable systems. Ultimately, this cohomology space is anticipated to play a significant role in the proposed monodromy representation. Networks (GANs) for creating realistic images, audio, and other data, they remain unreliable, often producing outputs that violate fundamental physical laws. For instance, GAN-generated images may feature birds defying gravity by flying unrealistically, creatures with excessive or misplaced limbs, or landscapes with impossible geographical inconsistencies. While current research addresses these issues in image synthesis by ensuring compliance with specific known constraints, general violations like extra legs are rarely caught. This paper introduces a novel framework for learning GANs that automatically identifies anomalies in produced samples and restores them to a valid manifold. Our approach relies on a discriminator that accepts two inputs: a sample and a correction vector. We train this system unsupervisedly by having the discriminator reject images with obvious violations, while teaching it to accept images with correctable issues by backpropagating losses from a generator aimed at minimizing a pre-trained anomaly discriminator. Consequently, this method yields checks for various anomalies and restores images with correctable violations. Experimental results demonstrate that images generated by this trained discriminator exhibit fewer anomalies than those from standard GANs. We successfully applied this technique to DCGAN, DCGAN-C, BRGAN, and DCGAN-GANMM on the CIFAR-10 dataset, observing that images with correctable anomalies were corrected. Furthermore, when combined with DCGAN-GANMM, anomalies were eliminated without degrading performance on a GAN's primary objective. Ultimately, we conclude that anomaly detection and image restoration can be achieved without any manual labeling. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first demonstration of self-supervised anomaly detection and image restoration within a GAN. This paper introduces FastTransformer, a novel architecture designed to utilize efficient convolutions for self-attention in image modeling while maintaining performance comparable to Transformer baselines. Specifically, fast self-attention in FastTransformer is achieved through Gated Linear Units (GLU), enabling parallel computation of queries, keys, and values through selective information gating. By replacing multi-head self-attention with GLU-based attention, we introduce two fast operator variants: LinearFast and StridedFast, which accelerate or downsample the attention query-key-value tensor, respectively. Our evaluation of FastTransformer on image classification tasks for ImageNet-1,000 and Stanford Online Products (SOP) demonstrates that our efficient convolution framework attains state-of-the-art results on all datasets while utilizing only one eighth to one third of the training parameters compared to multi-head attention models. Furthermore, fast models trained for 30 epochs on ImageNet achieve top-1 accuracy within one percent of deeper models that reached 96.3% accuracy after 100 epochs. We have made our code and models publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/FastTransformer. Additionally, fast models outperform state-of-the-art methods on SOP, marking the first time this approach has been extended to multi-label image classification. We anticipate that our fast models will be valuable for practical, large-scale, multi-label image classification tasks where low latency and high accuracy are critical. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/microsoft/SOP_fastmodels_pytorch. Our findings indicate that GLU-based convolutions effectively substitute multi-head self-attention in Transformers without sacrificing accuracy, while reducing the count of floating-point operations and trainable parameters by an order of magnitude. Fast models trained for 30 epochs on ImageNet within 3 days achieve 90.2% top-1 accuracy with 7.5M parameters, whereas deeper models trained for 100 epochs achieved 96.3% top-1 accuracy with 11M parameters. computational and storage demands of deep learning models. Although the literature contains numerous methods for enforcing weight sharing, very few provide theoretical guarantees, and existing analysis is often limited to specific scenarios. This study examines two storage-efficient strategies: random pruning, which removes weights randomly, and uniform pruning, which eliminates a subset based on their magnitude. We establish an error bound for both techniques that does not depend on the network's specific structure or the training dataset. Notably, even when the original weights are fixed, we treat the pruned weight matrix as a random variable and analyze its impact using a concentration of measure argument. These contributions represent one of the first attempts to provide theoretical justification for these storage-efficient approaches. Furthermore, we support our analysis with empirical evidence through an experimental section. Our findings indicate that uniform pruning generally surpasses random pruning in performance, aligning with existing empirical observations. We also document a fascinating phenomenon where certain networks demonstrate significant resilience to extensive pruning, a trait not shared by others, a trait we attribute to the sparsity structure learned during training. Finally, we present an information-theoretic argument explaining this behavior, drawing inspiration from the concept of channel capacity. This work aims to complement current empirical research by offering theoretical insights into how pruning influences the learning process. We hope this theoretical foundation will facilitate future research in model pruning. Our complete source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishgarg99/Pruning. While engaging, TQA demands significant time, expertise, and consistency, yet research indicates that clients and translators frequently exhibit inconsistency in their evaluations. This paper introduces TQA-Games, a framework for playing board games designed to simulate the essential skills required in TQA. We detail two specific games, Eja-GO and TQA-Sudoku, and present an initial user study involving 30 participants (consisting of 16 professional translators, 7 postgraduate students, and 6 non-English speakers) to evaluate these games in terms of usability, difficulty, and the correlation between game performance and real-world TQA capabilities. The study's main findings are as follows: (1) both games are easy to understand, effective for practicing core TQA skills, and enjoyable; (2) performance on either game correlates with actual TQA performance on professional MT output; and (3) individual game performance does not necessarily correlate with one another. In conclusion, TQA-Games serve as a valuable, game-based method for TQA training and assessment, particularly for helping users develop TQA skills. Millions and Powerball draw more participants, thereby raising the chance of multiple winners sharing the pot. Consequently, the share per winner declines, which diminishes the anticipated utility of these lotteries. I developed an algorithm to generate all possible sets of first-, second-, and third-place winners for these games, allowing for an calculation of the distribution of expected winnings and identifying scenarios where a single winner maximizes expected utility. My analysis of recent draws during this three-year period finds that single-winner outcomes occurred 13 to 37 times more often than the distribution of expected winnings would predict. I offer two potential explanations for this finding. Additionally, I present two sets of recommendations aimed at enhancing the expected utility of lotteries. A simulation demonstrating my proposed modifications is included in the accompanying code.

This study examines the large-charge expansion within the 3d $O(N)$ model, focusing on the asymptotic regimes where the number of components $N$ is either very high or very low. In these limits, the expansion parameters $\frac{1}{N}$ and the associated effective charges become small, enabling a perturbative series in powers of $\frac{1}{N}$ accompanied by logarithmic terms. We derive the leading-order scaling behaviors for scalar operators, particularly the composite charge-density operators. Notably, our results reveal a distinct scaling form for the specific heat in the high-$N$ limit, which contradicts predictions based on Monte Carlo simulations. Furthermore, the high-$N$ expansion is complemented by an expansion in powers of $N$ to explore the high-spin regime. In this context, we identify a conformal fixed point corresponding to the critical point of the weakly coupled photon theory, a phenomenon linked to critical phenomena in spin glasses. We demonstrate that this fixed point remains stable against perturbations arising from the new critical field and marginal operators, thereby extending the large-charge expansion to a broader class of field theories. Additionally, we identify the unstable fixed point that likely governs the scaling of the specific heat near the critical point of the 3d Ising model. Our findings regarding the specific heat in the high-spin regime align with established experimental and theoretical predictions. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the large-charge expansion around the Ising critical point. This work introduces a stable fixed point that establishes the ultimate scaling form for specific heat in various theories and establishes a viable expansion series that bridges the low and high-spin regimes. We anticipate that the methodologies employed here will prove applicable to other quantum field theories. We employ a diagrammatic Monte Carlo (DiMC) technique, which stochastically samples Taylor series expansions of the scattering amplitude to assess the impact of quantum fluctuations. Our findings indicate that quantum fluctuations can fundamentally transform the effective interaction between the impurity and the Fermi sea, resulting in the emergence of a bound state even when the bare interaction is purely repulsive. Conversely, we observe that when the bare attraction is weak, these fluctuations cause the bound state energy to shift towards zero. This phenomenon offers a potential explanation for the experimentally observed nonlinear drag [L. A. Kletskov et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 115, 176402 (2015)] within a spin-imbalanced Fermi sea. This efficient and highly convergent series expansion holds substantial value for diagrammatic scattering calculations. Finally, our crucial insights regarding effective interactions and nonlinear drag stem from a fundamental insight into the convergence characteristics of the DiMC technique. Abstract:
Motivated by applications in medicine science, we examine the theory of finite chromatic sets in Euclidean space, approaching it via topology. Utilizing persistent homology—a technique for analyzing geometric data clouds—we derive invariants derived from this theory that describe such sets. These invariants remain robust in the presence of noise; specifically, their persistence reflects the capacity to tolerate noise. We demonstrate that these invariants yield more precise information than those derived from Rips complexes. Using our implementation of these invariants, we successfully segment cancerous cells in blood cell microscopy images. More comprehensive code implementing these invariants will be available soon. Our work builds upon and extends previous research by the authors.

scheduling theory, particularly in the context of processor sharing systems where applications contend for a processor via multitasking schedulers. These schedulers allocate processing time to each task based on its specific weight, a mechanism originally designed for the Unix operating system and later extended to kernels like Linux and Real-Time Linux. Although theoretical research on multitasking preemption-free schedules demonstrated their impossibility, practical adoption has surged, leading to the investigation of preemptive variants and associated algorithmic challenges, such as maximizing the total discounted discounted throughput of a task set. This paper presents the first algorithmic and complexity analysis regarding the scheduling of a preemptive system with multitasking, under the constraint that preemptions are limited to a constant $T$. Specifically, we examine constant $T$-restricted preemption ($T$-PSP), an extension of non-preemptive scheduling, and provide nearly tight complexity results for maximizing discounted throughput, even when preemption delays are minimal (i.e., $T=1$). Furthermore, we establish nearly tight lower bounds on the performance of $T$-PSP schedules relative to the optimal schedule, even in scenarios involving a single preemption. In doing so, we also provide a novel and independent complexity-theoretic contribution by investigating constant $T$-PSP within the context of minimizing weighted completion times. This problem variant, denoted as $T$-MPSW, presents distinct challenges from the established constant-time preemptions ($T$-MPS) problem. We show that for $T=1$, an $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithm exists for $T$-MPSW, whereas for $T>1$, we prove that any polynomial-time algorithm cannot achieve an approximation ratio strictly better than $2^{T-1}$, assuming $P$ is not in $NP$. Notably, even in the case of $1$-MPSW, an exponential number of edge cases in the LP-relaxation must be resolved, with at least one infinite set of edge cases emerging at $T=2$. Alignments represent a cutting-edge method for identifying, locating, and measuring deviations in process executions (traces) relative to reference process models. However, alignments typically require complete process executions that span from start to finish, or at least prefixes of such completions. This paper introduces prefix alignments, which allow for conformance deviation analysis using incomplete or partial process executions, alongside their measures of cost, frequency, and support. The primary challenge in developing a prefix alignment algorithm is that deviations in prefix traces can result in infinite costs. To address this, we propose methods that assign prefix-specific deviation measures, though calculating the total cost remains infeasible due to potential infinity. Furthermore, various strategies for completing prefix traces are explored to enable deviation detection, noting that while total cost and frequency can be derived from these completions, support generally cannot, as it requires knowledge of all possible prefix completions. The paper also outlines a prefix alignment algorithm that operates directly on prefix event logs without necessitating process trace completion. We demonstrate the application and evaluation of prefix alignments using real-world event logs from different organizations. Our findings indicate that when process executions are significantly incomplete, traditional alignments fail to measure deviations, whereas prefix alignments successfully identify deviations from these partial traces. Additionally, a prefix alignment algorithm outperforms traditional alignments in scenarios involving moderately incomplete process executions. It is important to note that while our method is well-suited for measuring deviations, it is not directly applicable to mining for best- and best-practice alignments. As future work, we aim to investigate how to leverage prefix alignments within an iterative process mining framework to identify deviations that contribute to "green" (best-practice) and "red" (best-promise) alignments. Finally, generalizing prefix alignments to other deviation measures, such as those that allow for reset or skip reductions, is also addressed in this work. Software development and maintenance are inherently complex, often non-sequential processes where code modifications are suggested in discrete patches. When a new suggestion conflicts with a previous one, it indicates that both cannot be applied simultaneously, implying that at least one must be executed first. More intricate situations involve multiple suggestions where some pairs are incompatible. In such cases, it is crucial to identify which tasks can be performed at any given moment. This work addresses that specific issue. More broadly, it focuses on analyzing the different strategies available for applying a set of suggested code modifications. A core challenge here is that when the $i$-th suggestion conflicts with the $j$-th, neither can be implemented until at least one task preceding it in the sequence is completed. Even in this basic scenario, determining the strategies that maximize the probability of completing a suggested task at each step is non-trivial. The challenge becomes significantly more complex when conflicts arise where a task conflicts with multiple other suggestions. In such cases, the problem of evaluating and comparing different strategies is extremely difficult. Given a set of suggestions, the goal is to identify the strategy—among all possible options—that offers the highest probability of applying a suggested task at any specific moment. For a specific set of suggestions, all possible strategies can be enumerated, and their efficiencies calculated. Although this task is typically addressed using machine learning with predefined categories, defining complete and mutually exclusive categories is often impractical due to the subjective nature of subjects and the presence of multifaceted topics, particularly in fields like academic literature. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised learning framework that utilizes user feedback to refine category definitions and generate high-quality training data. Category selection is an essential component of cataloging digital documents, a critical step in information organization. To facilitate automatic document classification in digital library systems, we propose a semi-supervised learning framework that employs a UI category selection interface. This design enables users to correct category definitions and enables the category classification module to leverage these refined definitions. Our goal is to evaluate whether this semi-supervised approach can achieve better classification accuracy than (1) pure machine learning approaches that require exhaustive, manually constructed category definitions and (2) semi-supervised approaches where categories are derived based solely on assumptions about document topics. We assessed the classification performance of our framework by conducting a learning experiment to train the system, a practice session to evaluate usability, and a rigorous evaluation experiment to test classification accuracy. Our findings indicate that our framework offers significantly improved classification accuracy compared to both pure machine learning and semi-supervised approaches relying on manual category definitions. We conclude that implementing category selection as a category refinement process constitutes a promising approach for digital library classification systems. This study demonstrates that our framework achieves significantly better classification accuracy than previous methods. Additionally, we provide empirical evidence regarding the effort required for document categorization using our framework. We establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of "soft" matchings, thereby enabling the design of mechanism architectures that guarantee a "soft" matching outcome. Consequently, we present a mechanism architecture that ensures a unique "soft" matching "stable" matching with the minimal violation of "soft" preferences. Finally, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of such a stable matching with minimal preference violations and utilize this insight to construct a straightforward, efficiently implementable, and uniquely "soft" stable matching mechanism that is robust to external interference. This proposed mechanism is adaptable to various practical scenarios, including strict, soft, q-, stable, and optimal matching with external interference. Additionally, we introduce the concept of "soft" matchings and propose an algorithm to solve the soft matching problem, which we have already implemented and made open-source. This solution is particularly well-suited for the livestock industry, where the inherent "soft" nature of livestock production necessitates flexible matching strategies. By applying this method, the model ensures the optimal and efficient matching of cattle, thereby maximizing the utilization of cattle resources and enhancing the overall efficiency of the livestock industry. In conclusion, our research has made a significant impact on the field of soft matching, and we are committed to continuing this progress through our ongoing efforts. Our work has been widely recognized and cited in the scientific community, and we are dedicated to advancing the field through our continued research and development. Our approach utilizes an extended energy balance equation, which incorporates both heat and a term accounting for the work performed by order-parameter gradients. This facilitates a comprehensive analysis of how thermal fluctuations influence the nonequilibrium thermodynamic properties of the system. We demonstrate that for standard liquid crystals, the generalised heat capacity approaches zero as the external field intensifies, yet thermal fluctuations prevent it from reaching zero. Furthermore, we calculate the extended compressibility, revealing that it diverges at the coexistence point and assumes an infinite value in the high-field limit. Additionally, our findings indicate that the magnitude of thermal fluctuations aligns with atomistic predictions, suggesting that molecular dynamics simulations can accurately describe the thermodynamic behavior of liquid crystals. This study introduces a computational framework for studying laser-induced thermal convection, enabling the analysis of temperature distributions and convective patterns generated by lasers in both liquid and gaseous media. The model incorporates radiative heat transfer between a temperature field and the surrounding air, alongside a simplified representation of convective heat loss. H-STREAM calculates the minimum execution time required to complete an SPG, taking into account the periodic nature of stream operators and their associated timing constraints. The problem is modeled as a system of difference constraints, and its solution defines a execution region outlining feasible start times for each operator instance. By exploring this region, H-STREAM identifies the minimum execution time for an SPG. English to low-resource languages often produce a significant volume of unnatural and nonsensical output, termed hallucination. While recent studies have examined this issue across various tasks, the specific mechanisms driving hallucinations in NMT remain underexplored. To address this gap, we present a comprehensive framework that dissects and localizes such hallucinations within NMT translations. This approach integrates two novel metrics designed to quantify the severity and specific characteristics of hallucinations. Finally, we hope this research will advance both theoretical and practical advancements in the field of natural language processing. In this study, we introduce a novel simulation method for rotating turbulence within a periodic domain, utilizing vertical geostrophic stretching. This technique stretches the dominant vortices in the inertial range parallel to the rotation axis while maintaining geostrophic balance. Our results demonstrate that this method effectively replicates the geostrophic turbulence regime found in rotating stratified fluids, characterized by an isotropic inertial range in the horizontal plane, Rossby wave sweeping, and kinetic energy cascades that are scale-dependent anisotropic yet horizontal. Specifically, we examine spin wave fluctuations around the expected spin-liquid fixed point and the proposed narrow-liquid phase within a generalized model incorporating both bond and site disorder. Our results indicate that spin-wave theory fails to capture the quantum spin liquid phase, consistent with mean-field predictions, yet we observe that large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations do not align with the spin-wave description. This discrepancy likely stems from significant many-body effects that are absent in the spin-wave framework but are essential for the proposed spin liquid. We conclude that quantum Monte Carlo simulations are insufficient to distinguish between the proposed spin-liquid and disordered phases, thereby highlighting the necessity of experimentally realized quantum Monte Carlo simulations or other methods to resolve this issue. Additionally, we examine the narrow-liquid phase based on the combined effect of bond and site disorder and its relationship to the Griffiths phase. We find that while narrow-liquid phases are unstable in pure systems, they can be stabilized by introducing disorder. We also demonstrate that narrow-liquid phases correspond to a Griffiths phase, characterized by an exponential density of localized eigenstates and altered dynamical physical properties. However, deploying these models in real-world scenarios presents a significant challenge, primarily because of the high computational costs associated with API usage. This paper investigates the potential of distilling such models into smaller, cost-effective alternatives. While prior research has concentrated on distilling Transformer architectures into Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), we demonstrate that directly distilling to RNNs often fails to capture the full nuances of training data annotations. To overcome this, we propose a hybrid approach to the large-to-small transfer problem, DSTF-2, which enables the combined transfer of knowledge to both RNNs and Transformers. By training the small model concurrently with the large model for specific NLP tasks within a supervised setting, DSTF-2 facilitates the distillation of task-specific nuances. Experimental results on real-world NLP benchmarks show that our method produces models that are faster while maintaining competitive performance. Specifically, on the MultiNLI benchmark, a bidirectional LSTM trained with DSTF-2 matches the accuracy of a BERT model in just 0.15 seconds on a CPU. Additionally, a bidirectional GRU trained on the full corpus achieves 84% accuracy on the same benchmark in only 0.01 seconds using a CPU. Furthermore, a small Transformer trained with our proposed framework outperforms a pre-trained BERT model on the same dataset in less time. These promising outcomes suggest that DSTF-2 offers a novel pathway for the practical application of language model distillation. The code is accessible at https://github.com/amanarora/DSTF-2. While most existing semantic parsing systems depend on datasets annotated with logical forms, annotting large quantities of text is both costly and time-intensive. This paper investigates the application of transfer learning to semantic parsing. We observe that transferability relies less on sentence-meaning diversity and more on the richness of surface-to-deep word mappings. Consequently, we introduce a new transfer task focused on rich word embeddings, creating two specific datasets for learning: ConNet and EmeNet. ConNet utilizes mentioning networks to propagate semantic information across mentions of the same entity, while EmeNet employs embedding networks for continuous vector representation learning. This study presents the first investigation into the physical mechanisms behind QPFs by analyzing the light curves of the hyperluminous X-ray source (HLX) 4XMM J052908.4+002737 (HE0529-0027), observed with the NuSTAR satellite. Our analysis reveals that the amplitude of QPFs in NU20170517A correlates with the energy band, a finding that contradicts the standard disk instability model. Conversely, for QPFs in both episodes of NU001837A, the amplitude increases with frequency, a characteristic consistent with the hot accretion flow model. These results demonstrate that QPFs can serve as a valuable tool for distinguishing between the disk and radiative-reconnection models of HLXs. Additionally, we observed that both the amplitude and count rate of QPFs in HE0529-0027 varied significantly between episodes, a pattern that the hot accretion flow model can explain. Overall, these observations suggest that QPFs originate from the hot accretion flow around HLXs rather than the accretion disk. This conclusion aligns with the hypothesis that the hyperluminous state of HLXs is driven by radiative-reconnection events in the hot accretion flow, a mechanism that also accounts for the highly variable state of HLXs. Furthermore, these findings offer a novel explanation for the "double hump" spectral feature in HLXs. Given that recent X-ray observations of HLXs exhibit similar characteristics, our study provides strong support for the hot accretion flow model. Finally, we briefly discuss the implications of these results for the nature of HLXs. The data supporting these conclusions are available at https://github.com/WeiweiWang1993/NuStar-HE0529-0027. This study investigates how magnetic fields affect the rotation of binary systems, specifically comparing magnetized stars in such binaries against non-magnetized counterparts and single stars. The specific objective is to determine the impact of these interactions on systems involving early B-type stars, utilizing two distinct stellar evolution codes: the BACCHUS and MESA frameworks. Our findings indicate that in binary systems, tidal forces cause the non-magnetized primary star to spin up due to synchronization, whereas the magnetized primary experiences braking. Furthermore, we observe that magnetic fields significantly alter the evolution of single early B-type stars, particularly those of spectral types B0V and B0I, which can become synchronized within approximately 10 million years. This represents a substantial reduction in rotation evolution timescales compared to non-magnetized stars, potentially increasing the frequency of tidal disruptions, mergers, and the formation of compact binaries. Additionally, we note that the BACCHUS model exhibits braking behavior, whereas MESA demonstrates coupling, suggesting a need for further investigation into the specific physics of angular momentum transfer between stars and their surroundings. Finally, we conclude that incorporating the effects of magnetic fields is crucial for a more precise understanding of angular momentum transfer in stellar binaries. The survey covers a 1'x1' area at 0.88 mm, capturing emission from $^{12}$C$^{18}$O, $^{13}$C$^{18}$O, $^{13}$CO, and H$^{13}$CO. We modeled the observed CO $^{12}$ and CO $^{13}$ emission spectra using a three-dimensional radiative transfer framework. Our findings indicate that the peak CO abundance within the disk reaches approximately $10^{-5}$ relative to H$_2$. This result aligns with the absence of CO depletion in TW Hya, suggesting that either gas-phase chemistry or photodissociation of CO dominates in this environment. Furthermore, the CO abundance in TW Hya exceeds typical interstellar medium (ISM) values by roughly two orders of magnitude, driven by a higher carbon abundance and, more significantly, by CO's resistance to depletion compared to other molecules in ISM clouds. These observations corroborate our conclusion that CO depletion plays a negligible role in the TW Hya disk. Finally, the CO abundance in TW Hya surpasses that found in other CO-rich disks, such as HD 163296 and MWC 480, by at least a factor of two. This higher CO content in TW Hya may stem from its greater distance from the central star, resulting in lower UV radiation and minimal CO destruction. Additionally, CO in TW Hya exhibits a more uniform distribution than in CO-rich disks, likely due to a less pronounced radial temperature gradient in TW Hya. The observed CO column density in TW Hya matches predictions from a standard disk model, implying that CO is not depleted in dust grains. However, the CO-to-H$_2$ ratio in TW Hya is approximately 0.005, roughly 10% of the ISM value, which is lower than the ratios observed in CO-rich disks. This discrepancy may be attributed to CO being locked within icy grains in the outer regions of TW Hya's disk. These results offer valuable insights for interpreting CO observations across various disk regimes and for understanding CO chemistry in protoplanetary disks. constructing state observers for nonlinear systems remains a difficult challenge, often failing to produce a stable estimation scheme even for seemingly simple cases. This paper addresses these challenges by adopting a fresh approach to ordinary differential equation analysis—specifically, viewing trajectories as paths within a one-parameter family of compact metric spaces to examine continuity and smoothness. Leveraging this innovative perspective, we propose a general method for ordinary observer design that is applicable across various practical scenarios. Specifically, we extend the Hou and Salapaka (2009) exact linear observer design to a broad category of nonlinear systems, establishing explicit and verifiable conditions for their application. Furthermore, through careful selection of observer gains, we ensure that the proposed design maintains robustness against unmodeled dynamics and measurement noise, a feature often absent in traditional exact observer designs. The paper includes several examples demonstrating both the advantage and the applicability of the new design perspective. Finally, we illustrate how to adapt the design to account for Lipschitzian system noise and measurement noise, ensuring the overall observer scheme retains robustness in noisy environments. These theoretical contributions are supported by corresponding simulation results. Additionally, we introduce a visualization technique for ordinary time-varying observer designs, enabling the observation of the future evolution of estimation error trajectories. Through visual inspection of these trajectories, designers can intuitively and efficiently select appropriate observer gains, thereby accelerating the design process. This new gain selection method is especially useful for noisy observation settings. Moreover, the proposed scheme offers a fresh perspective on error dynamics analysis, providing a fresh viewpoint on error dynamics. We begin with foundational background and existing literature, followed by a review of trajectory continuity and smoothness from both classical and modern perspectives. This design approach is intuitive, straightforward, and versatile, serving as a valuable alternative in the noisy observation domain. Subsequently, we extend the design to handle Lipschitzian system noise, presenting a general scheme that ensures stability in the presence of such noise. For instance, standard analysis typically presumes that all clients finish computation and transmit updates within a single communication round, an assumption that fails in real-world scenarios involving varied client dynamics. Consequently, existing approaches often propose complex, heuristic-based strategies to manage such heterogeneous behavior. This paper demonstrates that federeral learning can, nevertheless, converge to an exact stationary point even in the presence of non-i.i.d. data by employing a straightforward, generic, and easily implementable algorithm. Under standard assumptions, we derive exact convergence guarantees for this method, revealing an elegant result: under conditions of bounded client heterogeneity, the total convergence error consists of two distinct terms. The first term represents the expected gradient estimation error arising from sampling only a subset of clients. The second term quantifies the impact of client heterogeneity, characterized by both intra-client and inter-client discrepancies. We validate these theoretical findings through numerical experiments. Our findings indicate that under heterogeneous conditions, federated averaging may fail to converge; however, momentum can be utilized to eliminate the heterogeneity-induced error term, enabling convergence. Furthermore, this error term proves essential for selecting the optimal learning rate to maximize the convergence rate. Overall, our theory establishes that, within a federated learning framework, efficient algorithms can achieve exact convergence to a stationary point by utilizing momentum and an appropriate learning rate. Numerical experiments confirm that applying these principles yields significant performance improvements. To our knowledge, this represents the first work to derive exact convergence rates for federated averaging under the practical assumption of heterogeneous client behavior. The observed reduction in both $M_s$ and $T_{\rm N}$ with increasing Cu doping is attributed to the dilution of the Cu sublattice. Furthermore, the Cu ion is identified as the magnetic carrier, evidenced by the linear decrease in magnetic susceptibility ($\chi$) with temperature ($T$) at high-$T$, which aligns with the inverse of the molar magnetic susceptibility ($\chi_M^{-1}$) trend. This linear $\chi_M^{-1}$ vs. $T$ behavior, characteristic of the Curie-Weiss law, indicates antiferromagnetic interactions between Cu$^{2+}$ ions. These findings were analyzed using the Curie-Weiss law and the 2D Heisenberg model. Given that the interplanar exchange interaction is weaker than the intraplanar exchange interaction, the system is classified as a quasi-two-dimensional Heisenberg antiferromagnet. The weaker coupling results in a $T_{\rm N}$ lower than the 3D Heisenberg critical temperature of 31 K. This optimization enabled us to attain a minimum achievable depth of 2 meters while maintaining a line pitch as fine as 250 $\mu$m. barrier for low-energy compound nucleus formation is typically lowered because the nucleus can be prealigned in one of the two directions defined by its deformation. **Purpose:** To differentiate between reactions occurring in prealigned versus preanti-aligned states, the angular distribution of emitted neutrons serves as a valuable metric. **Method:** We introduce a theoretical framework to analyze neutron angular distributions as a function of prealignment state and demonstrate how laboratory angular distributions are transformed into center-of-mass coordinates. Furthermore, we apply this method to examine how laboratory neutron angular distributions evolve with increasing prealignment, observing that preanti-aligned states generate characteristic dips in the laboratory angular distribution. **Conclusion:** These characteristic dips serve as a significant experimental signature for preanti-aligned states. Additionally, we illustrate how preanti-alignment influences laboratory neutron angular distributions during fusion-evaporation reactions at various excitation energies and spin values. We find that preanti-aligned states result in steeper angular distributions in the center-of-mass system but flatter distributions in the laboratory system. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings regarding preanti-alignment effects on neutron multiplicity and angular distribution measurements. **Impact:** This study establishes a method for identifying preanti-aligned states through laboratory angular distribution measurements, offering a useful tool for analyzing preanti-alignment effects on evaporation residue and pre-fission fragment production cross sections. Such knowledge regarding preanti-aligned states is crucial for accurately interpreting experiments involving pre-fission fragment production at excitation energies exceeding the fission barrier. Furthermore, determining preanti-alignment effects on evaporation residue and pre-fission fragment production cross sections remains a critical requirement for elucidating the mechanisms behind enhanced cross sections in deformed nuclei. We anticipate that the proposed method will facilitate the quantification of preanti-alignment effects on these production cross sections. for the cooperative non-covert communication (CoCoV) paradigm, where an encoder (actor) and decoder (critic) are neural networks that dynamically adjust to maximize communication rate while minimizing the probability of detection by two distinct non-covert receivers. We demonstrate that this approach surpasses traditional algorithm-design techniques, which typically yield suboptimal solutions due to necessary simplifications of the CoCoV problem. Extensive simulations across various system configurations show that our method improves the average non-covert rate by 44% to 86% compared to existing algorithm-design-based approaches. Furthermore, we establish a sufficient and necessary condition for the convergence of the proposed algorithm, which relies on the Lipschitz continuity of the detection probabilities with respect to the system parameters. Additionally, we prove that the algorithm converges to a unique fixed point under these conditions. To further ensure convergence when Lipschitz continuity cannot be guaranteed, we propose a modified algorithm, which we analyze using Lyapunov analysis, showing it achieves convergence to a fixed point within a converging range. Our proposed and modified algorithms exhibit robust convergence properties across diverse scenarios without requiring specific constraints on system parameters. Finally, we present numerical results confirming the convergence of both methods under varying system conditions. These findings are derived from simulations where the encoder and decoder weights are initialized to zero. We also present a theoretical framework demonstrating that the algorithm remains convergent under this specific initialization scheme. This theory further indicates that the algorithm maintains its convergence properties regardless of the initial weights of the encoder and decoder networks. Its general solution incorporates four arbitrary constants, yet the requirement for a scalar product necessitates that two of these vanish. Consequently, the viable scalar products are limited to two distinct cases: Stieltjes and modified Stieltjes. This paper presents a complete family of regular reducible DCHE scalar products in the Stieltjes form and addresses the corresponding scenario for the modified Stieltjes case. Furthermore, specific parameters within these families are calibrated to ensure a positive measure for both Stieltjes and modified Stieltjes types. Ultimately, these structured families of scalar products facilitate the derivation of moment-based characterizations for the associated moment problems. Additionally, we explore their connection to the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) of the reducible DCHE. Notably, the inclusion of a gamma factor significantly simplifies the analysis of the reproducing kernel, leading to a substantial reduction in the number of parameters. Finally, we examine a specific sub-family of this reducible DCHE family that closely resembles the face-pair face-flip reducible DCH equation, for which we also derive an appropriate characterisation. These findings hold significant relevance for the study of quantum probability measures linked to the generalized Dicke model. Additionally, we provide a discussion on how to extend the derived characterisations to handle shifts in the moment variable. These extensions are represented as reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces of generalized Bessel-type operators. Our approach leverages recent advancements in reproducing kernel theory for generalized Bessel-type operators, which have proven instrumental in advancing the investigation of specific quantum probability measures. This work represents the first step in exploring reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces of DCHEs within the broader Chihara theory framework for orthogonal polynomials. In this context, we investigate the specific sub-family of reducible DCHEs to elucidate the concept of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces for DCHEs, thereby facilitating future extensions to more general cases. Within this framework, we also derive a characterisation of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces for a specific sub-family of reducible DCHEs. This characterisation is formulated using general Bessel-type operators and relies on the positivity of a specific matrix linked to the problem. This approach is particularly advantageous for resolving the moment problem, as it allows for a reduction in the number of parameters through the use of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. sparse vectors, such as matrix completion, have garnered significant interest recently. This surge in attention is largely driven by the desire to improve statistical efficiency, a trend exemplified by popular techniques like robust principal component analysis and sparse canonical correlation analysis. Nevertheless, most existing approaches rely on convexification methods that suffer from high computational costs, particularly in large-scale scenarios. This paper introduces a class of inexact recovery algorithms designed for low-rank matrix recovery problems that incorporate additional row- and column-weighted sparsity-promoting penalties. By leveraging column-wise sparsity, these algorithms achieve accelerated convergence rates and enhanced statistical efficiency. We also adapt the well-known ADMM framework to fully address the resulting column-weighted sparsity-promoting subproblems. Furthermore, by integrating techniques from the TFOCS package, we propose a method to solve sparsity-promoting subproblems that fail to reach exact sparsity, while also implementing strategies for adaptive row- and column-weighting. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the proposed methods' superior computational efficiency and statistical performance compared to several state-of-the-art baselines. Universality (LFU) ratio, $R_\Sigma$, to investigate $\mu/e$ universality within $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions at $e^+e^-$ $B$-meson factories. This observable encompasses both inclusive and semi-inclusive muon-to-electron muon/tau ratios, specifically $R_{\mu,\Sigma}=\frac{\mathcal{B}(B\to X_s\mu^+\mu^-)}{\mathcal{B}(B\to X_s e^+e^-)}$ and $R_{\mu}^{(p)}=\frac{\mathcal{B}(B\to p K\mu^+\mu^-)}{\mathcal{B}(B\to p K e^+e^-)}$, alongside the corresponding lepton-charge reversed versions. Utilizing the QCD factorization approach, we calculate these and other related LFU ratios in heavy meson decays for various final-state configurations, obtaining values that deviate from the Standard Model (SM) expectations by approximately 10%. While experimental data is currently scarce, upcoming measurements at the $B$-factory facilities Belle II and LHCb are anticipated to yield significant insights into these ratios. Furthermore, we also present theoretical predictions for the antiparticle counterparts observed in $\bar{B}^0$ decays. Additionally, we estimate the expected $\mu/e$ and $\mu/\tau$ LFU ratios for $B\to D^{(*)}\ell\nu$ and $B_s\to D_s\ell\nu$ transitions, respectively, based on the QCD factorization framework. Our proposed SM range for these ratios is approximately 20% below unity. Consequently, experimental verification of these ratios, along with any deviations from the SM, can be achieved with significant statistical significance using the anticipated data volumes at LHCb and Belle II. Finally, we also provide predictions for muon and tau LFU ratios, respectively, in $B_s\to D_s\pi^0$ transitions. Our theoretical findings suggest that any deviation from the SM in these ratios would be approximately 10%, and we discuss the potential for testing this prediction. Our proposed set of LFU ratios, which are sensitive to various Beyond Standard Model (BSM) effects, offers a novel avenue for exploring new physics at the TeV scale. as networks of interconnected nodes. A central challenge in this field is determining how the macroscopic behavior of complex systems depends on their microscopic structure. A prominent method for addressing this is through ensemble averaging, which involves randomly sampling networks from a specific class and calculating observables as averages across these samples. This process is known as generating a network ensemble. Such ensembles are characterized by definitions that are either independent of specific network details or by specifying which network features are averaged. For instance, degree distributions can be defined without sample averaging, simply by setting $k(i)$ as the degree of node $i$ and $n_k$ as the total count of nodes with degree $k$.

This work derives network models from degree-constrained ensembles defined by the collection of degree sequences $\{\mathbf{k}=\{k(i)\}_{i=1}^{N}\}$ and $\{\mathbf{n}=\{n_{k}\}_{k=1}^{m}\}$. It provides a universal, data-driven framework for selecting network models from a given ensemble. Our approach is general and recovers the configuration model and model fitting as specific instances. It yields a universal objective function for networks generated from an ensemble and offers a unifying perspective on network modeling.

Our general objective function indicates that model selection should be based on a $\chi^2$ test comparing in-degree distributions. This differs from the standard "model fitting" approach, which typically relies on comparing degree distributions. Consequently, our general objective function distinguishes between model fitting and model selection. It also addresses the limitation in model fitting where the randomization process fails to explore the model space sufficiently to find the global optimum.

We apply this method to a set of real-world networks, demonstrating that our proposed degree-constrained ensembles are more discriminative. In a case study involving an electronics company, we show that our method identifies the underlying generative process more accurately than model fitting. Furthermore, our objective function is more sensitive to the specific properties of individual nodes, offering a more granular view of the network. Finally, we discuss the implications of this approach for both network science and machine learning. The source code is available at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/DCNets. eco-evolution) has gained significant traction, offering profound insights into the interplay between ecological and evolutionary processes, particularly regarding how evolution influences ecological system responses to external disturbances. However, these systems often involve complex, non-linear interactions, and the mathematical tools required to analyze them—specifically, deriving analytic expressions for dynamic behavior—remain underdeveloped. This study presents an analytic approach to calculate the key parameters of a widely used analytic model for eco-evolutionary dynamics: the adaptive dynamics equation. We first outline the fundamental approach and assumptions of eco-evolutionary models, followed by a demonstration of analytic methods applied to simplify and understand the core adaptive dynamics equation. Subsequently, we investigate the analytic behavior of these equations and their specific responses to perturbations. Finally, our work underscores the potential of analytic methods to investigate the mechanisms driving the interactions between ecological and evolutionary dynamics. These approaches may prove valuable for examining the intricate dynamics of evolving systems, including their reactions to perturbations, the formation of ecological niches, and the dynamics of emerging diseases. Achieving fully autonomous systems that can handle complex tasks in unstructured, real-world settings requires that any vehicle—whether ground-based or aerial—be capable of perceiving its environment, executing maneuvers, and making decisions autonomously. Liquid helium offers the highest known stability for achieving this low-temperature state, while the helium-free $^3$He-$^4$He diphasic system provides access to more extreme temperatures. This review examines the established fundamentals and recent advancements in the thermal and fluid-dynamic characteristics of both diphasic liquid helium and diphasic superfluid helium. Finally, the potential challenges associated with the extensive deployment of these cooling systems in third-generation low-frequency radio telescopes are identified. However, accurately and efficiently counting white blood cells and identifying their specific types remains a difficult task for pathologists.
