We show that the original leaf model is described by a specific set of variables paired with a corresponding set of evolution equations. By exploring an alternative set of variables, we derive a modified set of equations. This new set better aligns with the expected properties of a static, nonradiating, isolated black hole, suggesting it more accurately represents the genuine nature of stationary black holes. Thus, we argue that the original dynamical equation in the proposed leaf model may not solely describe the spacetime of an isolated black hole, but may instead account for some features of an nongravitational field. This conclusion was reached by utilizing the geometric approach, which serves as a foundation for understanding the nature of specific dynamical equation formulations. Our findings indicate that the appropriate selection of gravitational variables is crucial for gaining insights into the true nature of stationary black holes. In the zero-temperature regime, we derive an effective dimerized double-well Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian from a three-site system and analyze the resulting superfluid-insulator phase transition. At finite temperatures, the Mott insulating state is characterized as color superfluid or Mott color crystal, where the long-range order of the Mott gap corresponds either to the fluidity or lattice structure of the system. Beyond the mean-field approximation, we employ a time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory to explore the dynamical properties of Mott gap formation, identifying it as a first-order phase transition. Finally, we investigate how varying SOC strength modifies the phase transition temperature. This study offers an alternative approach to achieving effective lattice structures without conventional optical lattices and provides a foundation for investigating Mott physics through coupled spatial and spin orbitals. In conclusion, our work demonstrates the potential for investigating Mott physics using existing solid-state quantum devices equipped with spin-orbit coupling. This research contributes to the broader objective of developing spin-orbit-coupled superconductors featuring d-wave pairing symmetry and topological superconductivity. The thermal characteristics of the SOC-modified Mott state are also relevant to understanding high-temperature cuprate superconductors. Annealing experiments on cuprates indicate a competition between Mott physics and Cooper pairing, which can be interpreted through the framework of spin-orbit coupling. Annealing experiments on topological superconductors further reveal a competition between Mott physics and superconductivity. In numerous scenarios, the objective is to identify a kernel that facilitates efficient learning from training data to accurately predict on unseen examples. Furthermore, given the extensive number of kernels available, it is often impractical to evaluate all options. Induced Backgrounds (BIB) caused by in-flight muon decays occurring within the beam pipe and near the detector. These decays generate charged and neutral particles that degrade the reconstruction quality of primary interaction tracks. This study presents the initial characterization of this BIB within the 2020a configuration of the ILD detector at mu+e- colliders designed for Higgs and top quark physics. Utilizing the ILCDB simulation framework, we simulated mu+e- collisions at center-of-mass energies of 0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 3, and 16 TeV. The resulting BIB levels are shown to be severe, particularly in the far end-caps, where they can approach or surpass the signals from primary interaction events. While the BIB intensity scales directly with the primary Luminosity, the ILD design can maintain BIB contributions below 1% of the primary interaction events even at the 3,000 $\mu$m collision point. However, to achieve even lower BIB rates for the high-energy physics (HEP) collider mode, enhancements to the cryogenic far end-cap design are necessary. fundamental to many emergent quantum phenomena, including high-temperature superconductivity and the quantum Hall effect. This study examines many-body effects and their influence on emergent phenomena by comparing two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) systems. We investigate the interaction between a lattice of quantum dots and a reservoir of ultracold fermionic atoms in both 2D and 3D configurations. By varying the interaction strength and density within the quantum dot array, we observe two distinct emergent quantum phases in the 2D case that do not manifest in 3D. Specifically, when half-filling is approached, we identify phases characterized by interactions that are attractive rather than repulsive. Conversely, at low densities, interactions between the quantum dots become attractive instead of repulsive. These findings are explained by examining the energy shifts of the quantum dot array caused by reservoir interactions. Our results highlight the critical nature of dimensionality in systems involving quantum dots and reservoirs, as well as in broader contexts of lattice atoms coupled to quantum gases. Ultimately, this research deepens our comprehension of emergent quantum phenomena and enhances the potential for designing quantum devices based on quantum dot arrays. These arrays could serve as components for quantum information processors and superconducting circuits utilizing superconducting atoms or qubits. Additionally, they suggest the feasibility of implementing quantum simulations of emergent quantum phenomena and unconventional superconductivity using current experimental capabilities. This paper introduces a technique utilizing a resampling approach to evaluate the reliability of resampled signals for both cause-effect phase synchronization (cePS) and recurrence quantification analysis (RQA). Specifically, cePS measures the synchronization between two signals, while RQA analyzes the recurrence patterns of a single signal. When units possess distinct counterfactual potential, a trade-off emerges between the internal validity of relative treatment effects and the construct validity of absolute effects. This paper proposes an identification assumption that enables the estimation of unit-specific complementarity and substitutability, thereby expanding on the traditional binary view of heterogeneity in joint effects. By developing new estimation and inference techniques, I demonstrate that relative effects can be weighted to construct tailored indices of absolute effects—such as the average, harmonic mean, and geometric mean—each offering unique advantages regarding invariance to outcome scale transformations. These indices allow for unit-specific and aggregate measures of substitutability and complementarity to be derived from a single model, facilitating a more nuanced assessment of how internal and external validity objectives influence the choice of absolute effect metrics. Applying this framework to data on student test score responses to financial incentives reveals evidence of both substitutability and complementarity in the outcomes produced by schools, alongside substantial variation in how individual schools combine financial rewards to stimulate student performance. Furthermore, I present new evidence regarding the efficiency and robustness of various absolute effect measures. Specifically, relative effects can be aggregated to form indices that are less sensitive to heterogeneity in counterfactuals than either the arithmetic mean or the average of geometric means. Additionally, absolute means are robust to heterogeneity in internal complementarity and substitutability, whereas other indices resist external heterogeneity in complementarity and substitutability caused by scale transformations. Consequently, researchers can make an informed decision between adopting relative or absolute treatment effects based on their specific research objectives. Finally, I provide new estimates of the economic returns to public spending on K-12 education, accounting for the non-additive nature of student responses to these incentives. Nevertheless, some schools do exhibit complementarity in how students respond to spending, and I identify these institutions, offering policymakers practical guidance on how to optimally allocate spending. This study represents the first to estimate both types of complementarity, and it shows that absolute rates of response to spending are 40% higher when utilizing geometric means instead of arithmetic means. We introduce a set of theoretical results aimed at characterizing the typical set for common connected lengths of excursions within a generic one-dimensional Markov chain. Our findings include estimates for the entropy of the typical set, the time duration of excursions, and the connected length itself; the latter is characterized using a novel and independent method known as the first passage time profile. For the latter, we demonstrate that, with high probability, the statistics derived from the simulation of excursions align with those expected from the Markov chain formed by the lattice's elements, provided the Markov chains on both levels share the same connected excursion lengths. We further validate our theory by examining the first passage time profile, the time length of excursions, and the connected length in the context of the Potts model. Additionally, we present a correction for finite-size effects. The outcomes indicate a strong agreement between the theoretical predictions and simulation data across various temperatures and system sizes. This successful demonstration of our methodology in the Potts model suggests that the theory holds significant promise for broader applications in diverse Markov chains, given the model's extensive use in both theoretical research and practical scenarios. of research in recent years. In the context of a neural network classifier, an adversarial example is a perturbed input that causes a classifier trained on clean data to misclassify it. These examples often exhibit transferability, meaning they can deceive models with distinct architectures. This paper examines the characteristics of adversarial examples specific to handwritten digits. To achieve this, we introduce a method for estimating the region in the feature space where these examples exist. By applying dimensionality reduction and unsupervised clustering to features extracted by a standard classifier, we utilize the resulting distance metrics to identify the location of adversarial examples. This study investigates two types of perturbations: $F_{\infty}$-constrained and Black Box, with the latter demonstrating broader coverage. The proposed algorithm is evaluated on the MNIST and SVHN datasets. The experiment's primary goal is to determine which features a human would find most informative for classifying the digit in a given image. The results indicate that adversarial examples fall within a low-dimensional subspace of the original feature space. Additionally, the findings show that $F_{\infty}$ examples occupy a narrower space than Black Box examples. Finally, there is observed transferability between the datasets for both types of adversarial examples. We determine the maximum possible number of edges in such a hypergraph, denoted as $f(3,t)$, where $t$ represents the maximum number of vertices per edge. It is established that $f(3,t)$ does not exceed $t+1$. We conjecture that the only way to achieve the maximum number of edges is by using disjoint sets of 3 vertices, specifically 33 sets of two vertices and $(t-2)$ singletons. Under this conjecture, we prove that such a hypergraph exists for all $t \geq 4$. Additionally, the paper identifies and classifies all 3-intersecting hypergraphs that deviate from this specific structure. Finally, a separate section deduces that if a 3-intersecting hypergraph is not 4-intersecting, then the total number of edges cannot exceed $t^2+1$. Consequently, if a 3-intersecting hypergraph achieves exactly $t+1$ edges, it must necessarily be non-4-intersecting.

However, maintaining accurate ontologies is a significant challenge necessitating periodic revisions. Within semantic medical image analysis, for instance, an ontology might include a predicate linking a CT scanner to specific anatomical structures it is designed to visualize. When evidence emerges that this scanner also effectively images additional structures, the appropriate action is to create a new predicate connecting the structure to the scanner. This work introduces a method for semantic program synthesis aimed at support the efficient and consistent computer-aided revision of ontologies. Specifically, the approach automatically generates programs—specifically, the compositional semantic matching pipeline—to execute a new ontology predicate based on its semantic definition and an illustrative example. Furthermore, we have implemented a prototype system that utilizes this synthesis technique to automatically populate an image analysis pipeline with semantic annotations. These experiments demonstrate a reduction in the labor required for common ontology maintenance tasks by more than 80%, while the synthesized code ensures consistency and repeatability. Consequently, ontology managers can update ontology components with precise control over the meaning and functionality assigned to new predicates. In a broader sense, this research in computer-assisted ontology engineering offers a framework for utilizing well-chosen examples and expert knowledge to support the efficient and consistent maintenance of ontologies. Since correlation filters are lightweight and well-suited for face recognition, this paper introduces a correlation filter-based domain adaptation framework to address general agnostic False Positive Domain Shift (FPDS). To model correlation filters effectively, we employ an invariance-based model that captures both the content difference and content mixture of images. By leveraging invariance properties under FPDS, we demonstrate that the original image's correlation function changes under false positive attacks. We establish an explicit relationship between false positive images and the original content, revealing that original images and false positive images mixture images exhibit distinct characteristics in their correlation functions. Building on this insight, we propose an explicit model for correlation filter-based face recognition that successfully overcomes FPDS. The framework is fully unsupervised and easily extendable to other domain adaptation contexts. Experimental results confirm that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods. Additionally, the framework is highly deployable due to its ability to generate the model dictionary in just milliseconds using edge devices. Furthermore, the light-weight model enables the use of an ensemble of diverse, randomly initialized small filters, a strategy proven to be effective in standard domain adaptation literature. This combination of features offers the advantage of delivering high performance with low computational costs. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy and efficiency of our proposed framework. 1. Introduction
Text generation is a multifaceted challenge, yet it often begins with a simple string of characters. However, in many scenarios, the initial string lacks specific properties required for the final output. For instance, when generating an answer, the text might not meet certain criteria such as being in a particular language, containing a specific character count, or adhering to a certain style. In this paper, we investigate how to learn the process of transforming a generated string into one that satisfies these additional requirements. We focus on learning text transformation functions that map an input string to an output string satisfying a given constraint.

(b) Example of learning the internationalization function, which takes a US phone number (input) and transforms it into an international format (output).

Our contributions are as follows:
- We propose a general framework for learning text transformation functions that map input strings to output strings satisfying a specific constraint.
  1. The learning process is language-agnostic and capable of handling an unrestricted set of languages.
  2. The framework is versatile, applicable to both symbolic and natural language data.
  3. The learning process is straightforward to implement and does not require an explicit transformation function.
- We demonstrate that this framework can be utilized for multiple real-world NLP tasks, such as data generation and phone number internationalization.
- We illustrate that the proposed tasks can be framed as sequence to sequence transduction problems, which can be solved using high-dimensional neural networks.
- We validate our approach on several practical tasks, including data generation and phone number internationalization.

Nevertheless, automatic localization and identification often remain inaccurate due to factors including anatomical variations, image quality issues, and pathological conditions like vertebral tumors or spinal curvatures. This paper introduces a robust method for identifying vertebral regions of interest (VOIs) that performs reliably across diverse vertebral pathologies, varying image acquisitions, and vertebral grades. The proposed approach utilizes a cascade of three convolutional neural networks (CNNs) designed to detect vertebrae within spinal coronal CT slices. Each network is trained with hard example mining and employs a two-stage training process comprising a self-training phase followed by fine-tuning. Consequently, this method enhances detection accuracy and reduces both the computational memory requirements and processing time for each verification. Ultimately, the VOIs identified by this multi-CNN framework are incorporated into vertebral segmentation and identification pipelines. To our knowledge, this study represents one of the first to propose a vertebral detector based on CNN technology. Experimental results demonstrate that the detector reliably and accurately localizes VOIs across various vertebral pathologies, image qualities, and grades. In a test set of 250 coronal CT slices from 10 patients exhibiting diverse vertebral conditions, the detector identified 99.6% of VOIs, achieving a mean intersection over union of 0.85. Furthermore, the detector efficiently and accurately detected VOIs containing spinal pathologies in coronal CT slices with a mean intersection over union of 0.80. The supplementary material provides visualizations of the detected VOIs. Overall, the high reliability and accuracy of the detector, alongside its efficiency, make it well-suited for integration into vertebral segmentation and identification systems. Under conditions of ultrastrong coupling between electrons and the cavity's electromagnetic field, vacuum fluctuations induce the dynamical stabilization of a quasistationary polariton state trapped at the center of the repulsive potential. When the energy of an incident free electron falls within the energy gap, it is not reflected but rather resonantly absorbed to populate this stabilized state. This resulting pulse of the free-electron energy gap is theoretically modeled as the fermionic equivalent of a dynamical Casimir effect pulse in the electromagnetic field, termed the Casimir polariton pulse. The theory predicts the joint emission spectrum of this Casimir polariton pulse and the Casimir electric field pulse, demonstrating that the joint polarization state is entangled. We propose that this system serves as a platform for generating entangled electron-photon pairs. Additionally, we identify the joint orbital angular momentum (OAM) of the Casimir polariton pulse, offering a method to detect and manipulate the OAM of the electron wave packet emitted from a quantum vacuum. The proposed method for Casimir polariton generation and OAM detection may find applications in quantum information processing and quantum feedback control. The experimental setup requires only a laser-driven electron gun and a resonator, both of which are accessible technologies. This approach offers a new pathway for creating and manipulating the quantum states of fermions and photons. Specifically, it enables the generation of entangled electron-photon pairs via the joint polarization, presenting a unique method for quantum information processing. The proposed OAM detection method utilizes a quantum non-demolition approach, where the quantum state of a probe atom is entangled with the OAM of Casimir polaritons. This enables nondestructive detection of the OAM of the incident electron wave packet. These findings represent the first demonstration of ultra-high precision OAM detection for fermions, achieved through quantum entanglement. The proposed technologies for Casimir polariton generation and OAM detection could be realized using a simple cavity and existing electron beam equipment. This research represents the first step toward quantum information processing involving fermionic information. By demonstrating the quantum entanglement between electrons and photons, it paves the way for quantum information processing that directly utilizes the quantum properties of free-electron wave packets. This study holds significant potential for advancing quantum information science. The quantum entanglement between electrons and photons is a fundamental concept that will shape the future of quantum information processing. Consequently, this study investigates whether second-order cone programming (SOCP) can optimize the policy of multi-agent second-order dynamical systems, such as animal-like robots. We introduce SCOTTY, a synthesis algorithm that leverages the geometric properties of SOCP, the concept of set-based model predictive control (SCOTTY exemplifies this as a feedback control policy derived from SOCP solutions), and the universal approximation capabilities of neural networks. SCOTTY unifies safety and stability as a single constraint within its optimization framework. To solve the SOCP, we employ a dual-based approach that transforms the SCOTTY synthesis into a conventional convex problem using duality theory and Lagrangian duality. We assess SCOTTY on a multi-agent multi-neural-network (MANet) framework, where individual neural networks represent individual agents. During training, SCOTTY generates value sets for state and action cones at discrete time steps, which serve as target values for learning the MANet. At inference, these value sets are used to solve the SOCP and determine the agents' control actions. We evaluate this framework on a 14-agent scenario involving collision avoidance, coverage, and unstructured terrain navigation. Our findings indicate that, even after training for only 100 episodes, SCOTTY outperforms state-of-the-art learning-based methods in these tasks. Furthermore, we observe that the SCOTTY policy is capable of maintaining safety and stability for over 1000 seconds without retraining, demonstrating its suitability for real-world deployment. This study examines the tearing, coalescence, and coalescence saturation of microtearing modes within a WCOA (Weighted Circular Orbit Approximation) gyrokinetic framework, which incorporates toroidal effects, curvature, and passing/trapped electron sources. Our findings indicate that a WCOA-based gyrokinetic simulation necessitates an electron temperature gradient ($\nabTE$) exceeding the ion temperature gradient (ITG) threshold for microtearing saturation to occur. This behavior aligns with recent analytic predictions, which state that electron temperature gradients—whether they stabilize or destabilize the mode—directly enhance cross-field (canonical angular momentum-conserving) electron diffusion. We observe that the analytic analytic formula accurately predicts saturation levels for both magnetized and unmagnetized ITG scenarios. In the ITG-regime, we further demonstrate that the saturation of the resulting reconnected magnetic field is proportional to $|\nabTE|^2$, thereby amplifying curvature-driven instability and accelerating coalescence. These results have significant implications for turbulence modeling in tokamans and astrophysical accretion disks. Furthermore, this mechanism offers a potential solution to the long-standing issue of anomalous transport in stellar coronae, where temperatures reach millions of degrees. We anticipate that these results will facilitate more accurate modeling of turbulence in various plasma environments. However, current approaches typically depend on straightforward queries, such as image snippets or image sets, and offer limited support for complex queries or external knowledge. Furthermore, existing frameworks often prioritize accuracy over user experience, neglecting the human factors involved in interacting with image search systems.

To address these limitations, we introduce Knowledge Image Search (KIS), a system designed to enhance both the user experience and the handling of complex queries. KIS allows users to incorporate external knowledge, such as images retrieved from the web or personal photo libraries, into their searches. Additionally, the system improves the user interface by presenting suggested queries and utilizing natural language input to refine relevant results.

Our evaluation demonstrates that KIS boosts user engagement and session time. Statistical analysis confirms that users interacting with KIS spend more time exploring results and that the displayed search suggestions are effective. These findings indicate that integrating external knowledge and natural language capabilities significantly elevates the quality of the interactive session. We conclude that further research should focus on user experience design, particularly regarding how knowledge and natural language inputs influence user behavior and interface interactions. This approach offers a more comprehensive perspective on result relevance and helps bridge the gap between system accuracy and actual user satisfaction. By addressing both these aspects, we aim to advance the practical utility of image search solutions. Finally, we outline specific guidelines and future research directions to integrate knowledge into image search experiences. We believe that exploring these human-centric factors will be essential for the next generation of image search systems. We present our insights at the 2020 ACM International Symposium on Semantic-based Search (IC-SEM 2020). (2020). Subsequently, we analyze the scattering data, including wave numbers, discrete norms, norming constants, phase shifts, and continuous/spectral norms, distinguishing between periodic and quasi-periodic scenarios. Finally, we construct the inverse problem via Greenberg-Karney and Fokas-McIntosh methods for both periodic and quasi-periodic cases and utilize it to rebuild the original equations. Our findings indicate that the quasi-periodic solution encompasses specific features found in the periodic solutions, specifically the scattering states, background wave, and nonlinear phase. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the derived quasi-periodic solutions possess finite energy within a bounded region but lack the property of being solutions to the Cauchy problem. These findings offer a foundation for exploring the physical characteristics of the Fokas-Lenells equations. Additionally, we provide a Gravitational wave-based Hamiltonian formulation for these equations, drawing inspiration from the inverse scattering framework. This approach not only recovers the original equations but also yields a new set of equations featuring novel properties. The applicability of the finite-group method is confirmed, and the derived Hamiltonian framework offers a more efficient basis for analyzing the finite-dimensional phase space of the equations. Given that this work extends the analysis of the Fokas-Lenells equations, the developed scattering theory and Hamiltonian framework are also pertinent to other integrable nonlinear partial differential equations with Lax pairs. To demonstrate the theory, we apply it to various scenarios, including periodic and quasi-periodic cases, showing that the derived Hamiltonian yields more elegant results and better illustrates the finite-dimensional nature of the phase space. The primary applications of the Hamiltonian derived via inverse scattering analysis involve solving equations with initial-boundary value problems and enhancing the understanding of boundary effects on nonlinear waves. The proposed Hamiltonian framework is anticipated to be applicable to other integrable nonlinear PDEs as well. To conclude, the inverse scattering analysis in this study not only advances the theoretical understanding of the finite-scattering quasi-periodic Lax pairs and their associated equations but also provides a novel approach for solving them. for investigating quantum gravity characteristics and establishing a rigorous environment to examine condensed matter systems exhibiting non-relativistic symmetry. Within these theories, the dynamical action incorporates geometric quantities derived from two distinct connections: the Christoffel connection, which relies solely on the metric, and an additional independent connection known as the nonlinear connection, which influences the effective degrees of freedom and influences the conserved quantities. This study analyzes the theoretical characteristics of Dirac fermions within a nonlinear gravitation model where the nonlinear connection is decoupled from the Riemannian structure. To derive the gravitational analog of the Pauli equation, we employ a teleparallelism-based approach that utilizes tetrads and connection coefficients. We achieve this by performing a generalized gauge transformation on the connection and subsequently applying a non-invariant Lorentz transformation, thereby decoupling the Christoffel connection from the nonlinear one. Furthermore, we derive the gravitational version of the Pauli equation for Dirac fermions in the presence of this nonlinear gravitation model, which accounts for both the Christoffel and nonlinear connections. We demonstrate that the effective equation of motion for the spinor can be recast into a Schrödinger-like equation resembling the non-relativistic Hamiltonian of Dirac theory, augmented by gravitational effects analogous to the spin-connection term found in the standard relativistic Dirac equation within Riemannian geometry. Finally, we derive the corresponding effective energy equation, which reveals insights into the unique theoretical properties of these nonlinear gravitation models. Additionally, we examine the specific case where the nonlinear connection represents a Ricci-flat connection, which holds particular relevance for the quantization of gravity. In this scenario, the effective equations of motion for the spinor simplify to those derived in the standard relativistic formulation involving the Christoffel connection and the associated Ricci gravitation theory. networks, this research investigates the deployment of reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) to enhance wireless performance within indoor environments. By utilizing metasurfaces to mirror and shape electromagnetic waves, RIS can transform the propagation characteristics of physical radio waves. Specifically, this study evaluates the RIS-assisted 802.11ax WiFi standard by evaluating a single-user scenario where an access point (AP) communicates with a stationary user equipment (UE). The UE remains connected despite a significant signal blockage, relying on a passive RFID-enabled RIS for assistance. For both RIS-enabled and RIS-disabled scenarios, the UE and AP evaluate transmission through numerous RIS configurations to determine the optimal surface. Results indicate that without RIS, the UE cannot successfully transmit through the channel blockage. Conversely, with a fixed RIS configuration, transmission is achievable. By implementing a joint configuration selection protocol for the RIS and the 802.11ax network, the system can automatically identify the best possible configuration among all options. This approach demonstrates consistent throughput improvements across various configurations, yielding up to a 3.2x increase for the 1MBps protocol, approximately a 2x increase for the 2MBps protocol, a 2.2x increase for the 3MBps protocol, and a 1.5x increase for the 4MBps protocol. Furthermore, the paper discusses the energy efficiency of the proposed solution. Although the UE expends additional energy to evaluate multiple RIS configurations, the substantial throughput gains result in an overall energy efficiency improvement of at least 1.2x. Finally, the study examines the impact of UE and AP locations, as well as the number of RIS reflectors, on performance. Analyzing these factors helps identify the most suitable deployment conditions for RIS in indoor settings. Overall, this paper paves the way for making RIS a practical reality in indoor communications.
